subject: Private deployment: connectivity options (PrivateLink / Peering / S2S VPN) for Odin Health
messages:
From: Alexis Park <alexis@odinhealth.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>, Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 14 Mar 2027 09:12:03 -0400
Subject: Private deployment connectivity options for Odin Health

Hi Soojin / team,

Thanks for the initial conversation at the demo. Odin Health is moving toward a Private deployment (VPC in our AWS account + Redwood Private in your VPC) and the security team has asked us to evaluate connectivity approaches: VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a site-to-site VPN. Key constraints:
- Strict PHI controls (SOC2 & HIPAA) — we need minimal internet exposure and strong auditing.
- Expected steady-state traffic: ~60 req/s with occasional bursts; typical RTT requirement is <40ms for inference.
- We prefer a solution that allows selective exposure (some services only) and easy tenant isolation.

Could you please provide a recommendation, quick tradeoffs (latency, ops complexity, cross-account setup, certificate/KMS considerations), and a suggested PoC plan + timeline? I attached our network inventory.

Attachment: network-inventory.csv (stub)

Cheers,
Alexis Park
Head of Platform Integrations
Odin Health
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
To: Alexis Park <alexis@odinhealth.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>, Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 14 Mar 2027 11:45:10 -0400
Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity options for Odin Health

Alexis — thanks for the details and the inventory. High-level guidance up front: PrivateLink (endpoint services) + S2S VPN for fallback usually gives the best balance for regulated customers who want isolation and limited surface area. Short bullets:

- PrivateLink (recommended primary)
  - Pros: fine-grained exposure (per service), cross-account semantics are explicit (service owner publishes endpoint), avoids routing table changes in customer VPC, better for multi-tenant isolation.
  - Cons: per-endpoint costs, additional ENIs in customer account, requires published endpoint service and support for TLS mutual auth or token-level controls.

- VPC Peering
  - Pros: simple L3 connectivity, low data cost inside region, good for high-throughput flows.
  - Cons: flat network visibility (harder to restrict to specific services), route table limits and potential cyclic-peering complexity across multiple customers, cross-account IAM work required for some setups.

- Site-to-site VPN
  - Pros: fast to stand up for PoC, minimal changes to customer cloud infra, good for initial validation.
  - Cons: latency/throughput variability, higher ops overhead long-term, maintenance of tunnels and keys.

Questions to size the recommendation:
1) Which cloud + region (AWS/Azure/GCP)?
2) Peak sustained bandwidth (Mbps) and burst window?
3) Any Egress inspection requirements (proxy / TLS intercept)?

I attached a short initial evaluation with decision criteria. If you confirm answers above I can draft a PoC plan and cost ballpark.

Attachment: initial-connectivity-eval.pdf (stub)

—Soojin

Adding some technical detail on tradeoffs and implementation constraints (quoting Soojin for context):

> PrivateLink (recommended primary) — per-endpoint costs, ENIs in customer account, requires published endpoint service and support for TLS mutual auth or token-level controls.

Some engineering notes:
- Latency: PrivateLink will add ~1–3ms overhead vs. same-region peering (mostly ENI hop). For your <40ms requirement it's fine unless you have very tight tail latencies under burst.
- Throughput: Interface endpoints are backed by ENIs; for very high throughput we should validate NIC and ENI limits in the customer's account and consider cross-AZ scaling of the endpoint service. I've put rough numbers in the attached workbook.
- Authentication: We recommend mTLS at the application layer and using customer-managed KMS keys for any envelope encryption. PrivateLink doesn't inherently solve auth — it reduces network exposure.
- Monitoring/audit: Need flow logs + endpoint service logs. We'll ask Odin to enable VPC Flow Logs and share CloudWatch/CloudTrail read-access (read-only role).
- Route/scale ops: Peering scales well for flat, high-throughput pipes but makes least-privilege network segmentation harder. Peering also complicates multi-customer topologies (transitive routing isn't allowed).

Recommended PoC (technical):
1) PoC v1 — Stand up S2S VPN between Redwood PoC gateway and Odin test VPC; validate request/response, latency, and auditability (2–3 days).
2) PoC v2 — Publish a Redwood PrivateLink endpoint service in us-east-1, have Odin create interface endpoints in test VPC, validate end-to-end encryption, auth, and scale (4–7 days).
3) Ops handover — share runbook for rotation of certs/keys and CloudWatch dashboards (2 days).

Attachment: bandwidth-estimates.xlsx (stub)

I'll also outline the IAM role we'll request for read-only logs and the minimal set of Security Group rules.

—Marcus
Marcus Lin
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity options for Odin Health

Thanks — useful detail. Quick answers:
- Cloud/region: AWS us-east-1 (single account for now).
- Peak sustained: ~60 req/s at 250ms avg payload size — estimate ~120 Mbps sustained with spikes up to 400 Mbps for short windows (30–60s).
- Egress inspection: we run a perimeter proxy for DLP; TLS termination is not permitted at the proxy (we only allow SNI inspection). We will need to ensure Redwood's endpoints can be reached without TLS interception.

Two asks before we book a PoC:
1) Rough monthly delta estimate (PrivateLink vs Peering vs VPN) given the bandwidth numbers above. Ballpark is fine.
2) A 2-week PoC timeline we can present to our security/compliance team.

Attachment: compliance-checklist.docx (stub)

—Alexis
From: Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>
To: Alexis Park <alexis@odinhealth.com>
Cc: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 16 Mar 2027 09:00:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity options for Odin Health

Alexis — thanks for the bandwidth numbers. Based on those and security constraints we recommend the following path and a concrete PoC timeline: 

Decision (recommended): Primary: AWS PrivateLink endpoint service + mTLS and customer-managed KMS. Secondary: S2S VPN as cold-standby for large bursts or troubleshooting. Rationale: PrivateLink provides per-service access controls (meets your reduced surface-area ask) while S2S VPN covers burst scenarios and gives a rapid fallback during the PoC.

Estimated monthly delta (ballpark, us-east-1, based on ~120Mbps sustained / spikes to 400Mbps):
- PrivateLink: AWS endpoint data processing + ENI costs + Redwood egress: ~ $2,200–$3,500 / month (depends on endpoint count and negotiated egress).
- VPC Peering: lower AWS charges for intra-region data transfer, but requires route management and broader network exposure; ~ $1,200–$2,000 / month.
- S2S VPN (managed): lower fixed infra costs but bandwidth-based charges and more ops; ~ $900–$1,800 / month (note: throughput and stable latency are variable).

2-week PoC timeline (compressed):
- Day 0–1: Kickoff + share minimal IAM role for read-only logs + test VPC details.
- Day 2–4: Stand up S2S VPN for quick validation (round-trip tests, flow logs).
- Day 5–11: Publish Redwood PrivateLink endpoint service; Odin creates interface endpoints in test VPC; validate auth (mTLS), KMS handshake, and 100–400Mbps stress tests.
- Day 12–14: Run audit checklist, capture logs, run failover to VPN, and handover runbooks.

Action items & owners:
- Odin: provide test VPC, CloudWatch/Flow Log role (due Day 1)
- Redwood (Soohjin/Marcus): publish endpoint service, run stress tests, produce runbook (Day 5–11)
- Redwood (Monica): project coordinator, procurement contact for egress negotiation and DocuSign for PoC agreement.

Next step: Can we schedule the kickoff for Monday next week? I’ll prepare the DocuSign PoC agreement and the minimal IAM role request.
